paras: The lynching of Jim Sanders was the shooting of a Black youth of about 18 by masked men in Union township, Arkansas, about ten to twelve miles from Little Rock, on the night of May 28, 1882. Sanders had been arrested that afternoon on an accusation of attempting to assault a white girl and was held under a constable's guard when the band broke in and killed him. The killing angered Black residents of the area, and Little Rock papers reported fears of a clash between white and Black residents in the following week.

According to the Little Rock Democrat, on the evening of Saturday, May 27, Nannie Carr, the ward of R. S. Parker, went to Parker's schoolhouse to prepare it for Sunday services. The Democrat said that Sanders crept into the building and seized her, while a New Orleans Times-Democrat special added that he carried a gun, asked for a drink and threatened to kill her if she cried out. Her screams drew William Pinson, who, by the Gazette's account, fired Sanders's own shotgun after him as he escaped.

Sanders made his way to Little Rock, where Chief of Police Counts arrested him at about two o'clock on Sunday afternoon at Main and Eighth streets. Deputy Constable Carter Walls and a posse took him back to Union and delivered him to Magistrate McAllister, who placed him in the charge of Constable Monroe Bowen. He was lodged in a small house near the mill, described elsewhere as a frame building near Parker's store, to await a hearing.

That night masked men broke into the building, overpowered the guards and shot Sanders many times, killing him instantly. The Democrat put the time at ten o'clock, while the Times-Democrat special and a Chicago wire said about midnight. The Little Rock Gazette wrote that enough buckshot to kill a score of men was lodged in his body.

Deputy Sheriff Botsford and Coroner Woolford left for the scene the next morning, and an inquest was held that day; no verdict appears in the coverage. An Illinois paper reported that some of the masked men were said to have been recognized and would likely be indicted, but no report of an indictment or trial was found.

Black residents of the neighborhood were described as "greatly excited and incensed," and threats of further trouble were made at the inquest. Magistrate McAllister told the Democrat he feared "a collision between the whites and blacks," though the paper expected none. On the following Sunday, white families near Wrightsville and Sweet Home hid in the woods on a rumor that Black residents were arming, while Black residents heard that their church had been fired into and two worshippers killed. The sheriff investigated and found the alarm to be "a groundless scare," according to the Gazette.

The Little Rock Democrat's account ran in the Memphis Public Ledger under the headline "SWIFT RETRIBUTION," and a Times-Democrat special reached the Brookhaven Ledger as "A Negro Attempts an Outrage, and is Lynched by a Mob." Wire briefs from Little Rock appeared on May 30 and 31 in Savannah, Yankton, Rock Island and St. Paul under headings such as "Riddled with Bullets," "LYNCH LAW" and "A Negro Ravisher Shot." The Chicago wire called Sanders "guilty" of the attempt, and most reports stated the accusation as fact rather than as a charge.

The Ottawa Free Trader in Illinois ran a fuller summary on June 3 headed "Summary Vengeance," which alone mentioned that members of the mob might be indicted. A week later the Gazette described Sanders as "shot and killed while in the hands of officers of the law" in a column reprinted by the Memphis Daily Appeal.

Reports varied on details: the Democrat placed the scene about twelve miles down the river and the killing at ten o'clock, while other dispatches said ten miles south and about midnight. The victim appeared as Jim Saunders, James Sanders and Jno. Sanders, and the girl as Nannie Carr, Nancie Carr and Nannie Corrie.

accounts.label: Little Rock Democrat

accounts.label: Times-Democrat special
accounts.gist: Sanders, carrying a gun, asked for a drink and seized Carr by the throat; held in a frame building awaiting a hearing, he was shot about midnight by masked men; an inquest followed amid Black anger.

accounts.label: Little Rock Gazette
accounts.gist: Pinson fired Sanders's own shotgun at him; Sanders was 'sent back for identification' and killed with buckshot after the guard was overpowered; later described him as killed 'while in the hands of officers of the law'.

accounts.label: Chicago wire
accounts.gist: A 'negro boy' 'guilty' of an attempt was lodged in the calaboose and riddled by masked men at midnight; Black residents were incensed.

framing.detail: The Memphis Public Ledger headed the Democrat's account 'SWIFT RETRIBUTION' and the Yankton paper 'A Negro Ravisher Shot', treating the accusation as proven.
Northern papers ran short wire briefs under 'LYNCH LAW', 'Riddled With Bullets' and 'Summary Vengeance'.
The Little Rock Gazette's later note said Sanders was 'shot and killed while in the hands of officers' and called the following panic a 'groundless scare'.
